# Embedded subgroup transport and exact extension counting

**Theorem.** Let \(G,G'\) be finite \(p\)-groups given by Cayley tables, every subgroup generated by at most three elements having class less than \(p\), and let \(H_1,\ldots,H_k\le G\) and \(H'_1,\ldots,H'_k\le G'\) be ordered lists of actual subgroups. The subgroups may be nonnormal, may intersect each other, and need no splitting hypotheses. There is a deterministic many-one reduction of their relative isomorphism problem to unmarked class-two \(p\)-group isomorphism on Cayley tables. When group orders and matching subgroup orders agree, put \(N=|G|=|G'|\) and \(P=\prod_i |H_i|\). The query groups and all intermediate tables have order \((NP)^{O(1)}\) with an absolute constant. In particular the queries have order \(N^{O(1)}\) for every fixed number of marked subgroups, and also whenever the product of the subgroup orders is bounded by a fixed power of \(N\). Relative search, exact counting, and automorphism generation deterministically Turing reduce to the same class-two decision oracle under the same bound. The results apply to arbitrary finite odd-order class-two groups by their Sylow direct decompositions.

One can also return generators for the restriction image on \(\bigsqcup_i H_i\). Given a proposed list of isomorphisms \(H_i\to H'_i\), this gives an extension test, an explicit extension when one exists, and the exact number of extensions. In particular the class-two oracle computes the size of the automorphism orbit of an actual embedded subgroup and determines whether two embedded subgroups lie in the same orbit, without enumerating candidate subgroups. The theorem includes mixed exponents and arbitrary actual subgroups of odd-order class-two groups. At \(p=2\) the class hypothesis in this theorem only covers abelian groups.

The main step is a subgroup-marked extension of the earlier associative Peirce encoding. The second step uses the all-class-two black-box search and automorphism theorem on the resulting groups. To pass generators back, a normalization must be independent of the inner conjugations used to recover ring corners. That independence is proved in Section 4. [Earlier ordinary class-two oracle theorem](https://github.com/Dugongue/MathProofs/blob/main/GrochowResearchSynthesis/CLASS-TWO-BLACK-BOX.md) · [Earlier Lazard class reduction](https://github.com/Dugongue/MathProofs/blob/main/GrochowResearchSynthesis/LAZARD-CLASS-REDUCTION.md) · [Published exponent-\(p\) class reduction, Grochow–Qiao Part IV §7.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2306.16317#S7.SS2)

## 1. From actual subgroups to additive marks

Use the Lazard Lie ring \(L=\log(G)\) with the same underlying set as \(G\). This correspondence preserves maps and restricts to subgroups. One can see the restriction directly from the implementation of the Lie sum and bracket as words in \(x,y\) and their inverses, using integer powers with coefficients reduced modulo the exponent. The degree-by-degree word construction in the cited Lazard class reduction gives these words in polynomial time in the Cayley-table order, uniformly when \(p\) varies. It uses all noncommuting words through degree at most \(c\) in two symbols and the inverse of \(1,\ldots,c\) modulo \(p^e=\exp(G)\), so the cost is \(2^{O(c)}\operatorname{poly}(\log |G|)\) for each pair. The bound \(c\le \log_p|G|\) is sufficient. Polynomial table construction also follows for each represented subgroup. Thus the same subsets \(H_i\) become additive submodules of \(L\) that are closed under the Lie bracket. They can be used as additive marks since the ambient map already has to preserve the bracket. No choice of a basis of \(L\) compatible with all marks is required. For abelian groups one may simply use the original addition and the zero bracket. Section 6 gives the same correspondence under the stated local class hypothesis, including when the entire group has class at least \(p\).

Reject mismatched prime, exponent, or order immediately. Likewise reject mismatched marked subgroup orders or exponents. Trivial marks can be removed in matching pairs. The trivial ambient group is decided directly. Write \(R=\mathbb Z/p^e\mathbb Z\) and \(R_i=\mathbb Z/p^{a_i}\mathbb Z\), where \(p^{a_i}=\exp(H_i)>1\). Run the construction for matching data below. The same procedure applies to any finite \(p\)-primary Lie ring with additive subgroup marks, even when no corresponding group has been given.

## 2. The associative ring with embedded subgroup marks

A named vertex \(v\) denotes an idempotent \(e_v\). A corner \(i\to j\) is the additive module \(e_iAe_j\), with its prescribed left and right scalar actions. Use seven core vertices \(s_0,s_1,m_0,m_1,m_2,t_0,t_1\), each with diagonal ring \(R\). The nonzero core off-diagonal corners are given below. Different occurrences denote different copies.

| Module | Corners |
|---|---|
| \(L\) | \(s_0m_0,\ s_0m_1,\ m_0t_0,\ m_2t_0,\ s_0t_0,\ s_0t_1,\ s_1t_0\) |
| \(R\) | \(s_0m_2,\ s_1m_0,\ s_1m_2,\ m_0t_1,\ m_1t_0,\ m_1t_1\) |

Specify the following off-diagonal products of composable pairs.

| Triple of vertices | Product |
|---|---|
| \(s_0,m_0,t_0\) | \((x,y)\mapsto [x,y]_L\) |
| \(s_0,m_1,t_0\), \(s_0,m_0,t_1\), \(s_0,m_1,t_1\) | \((x,a)\mapsto ax\) |
| \(s_0,m_2,t_0\), \(s_1,m_0,t_0\), \(s_1,m_2,t_0\) | \((a,y)\mapsto ay\) |

For each marked subgroup add a vertex \(w_i\) with diagonal \(R_i\). Give \(s_0w_i\) the module \(H_i\) and \(w_it_0\) the module \(R_i\). Their product in \(s_0t_0=L\) is \((h,a)\mapsto a h\) via the given inclusion. Add the directed path \(w_i\to w_{i+1}\) with corner \(\mathbb Z/p^{\min(a_i,a_{i+1})}\mathbb Z\). Its purpose is to order the marker vertices. Add a hub with diagonal \(R\), a corner \(R\) to each of the seven original vertices and a corner \(R_i\) to each \(w_i\). Number the seven core vertices from 1 to 7 in the displayed order. Give vertex \(j\) exactly \(10j\) pendant leaves, and give the hub \(2k+100\) pendant leaves. Each leaf and its incident corner use \(\mathbb F_p\). Give every off-diagonal corner its natural scalar actions from the two endpoint diagonal rings. Every unlisted off-diagonal product is zero. The sum of the vertex idempotents is the identity.

This is an associative ring. Every nonzero product of two off-diagonal elements lies in one of the final output corners \(s_i t_j\), and every further product with any off-diagonal corner is zero. Composability of corners and the balanced scalar actions verify products involving diagonal factors. In particular an element of \(R_i\) acts on \(H_i\) independently of its representative, and the inclusion into \(L\) preserves this operation.

The \(p\)-multiples of diagonal elements together with all off-diagonal corners form a nilpotent ideal. Indeed off-diagonal factors can appear at most twice in a nonzero product, and diagonal factors lying in the ideal each supply a factor of \(p\). The quotient by the ideal is the product of one \(\mathbb F_p\) for every vertex. Thus the ideal is the Jacobson radical \(J\). Any ring isomorphism or anti-isomorphism permutes these residue factors and the corresponding ordered Peirce corners, after conjugating a complete primitive idempotent system to the named one. For completeness, when \((f_i)\) and \((e_i)\) lift the same complete residue system, \(u=\sum_i f_i e_i\) is congruent to 1 modulo \(J\), hence a unit, and \(u e_i=f_i u\). Thus the corner pattern can be read from the ring without choosing an invariant system of lifts.

The directed graph of nonzero off-diagonal corners distinguishes all important vertices. The hub's out-degree \(3k+107\) exceeds every in-degree and every other out-degree. Reversing the graph would change its maximum out-degree, so no anti-isomorphism can occur between two rings of the stated format. Each core vertex \(j\) has its unique count \(10j\) of outgoing degree-zero endpoints. The remaining nonleaf vertices other than the hub are precisely the \(w_i\), ordered by their path. Each is therefore distinguished. Central elements commute with all the \(e_v\), hence are diagonal. Commutation with each cyclic scalar corner from the hub shows that the diagonal value at its endpoint is the residue of the hub scalar. The leaf corners give the same statement for the remaining vertices. Consequently the center of \(A\) is a copy of \(R\), a local ring.

## 3. The group query and correctness

An idempotent-preserving isomorphism \(A(L;H_i)\to A(L';H_i')\) has maps \(X,Y,Z\) on the three core \(L\)-corners \(s_0m_0,m_0t_0,s_0t_0\). Set \(a=uv/w\), where \(u,v,w\) are the scalar units on \(m_1t_0,m_0t_1,m_1t_1\), respectively. Set \(b=u'v'/w'\), where \(u',v',w'\) are those on \(s_0m_2,s_1m_0,s_1m_2\). The scalar triangles give \(Z=aX=bY\). The bracket triangle yields \(Z[x,y]_L=(ab)^{-1}[Zx,Zy]_{L'}\). It follows that
\[
f=(ab)^{-1}Z
\]
is a Lie-ring isomorphism. The product \(s_0w_i\) by \(w_it_0\) has image precisely \(H_i\) in the \(Z\) corner. Hence \(Z\) sends this image onto \(H_i'\). Applying the overall unit scalar leaves \(H_i'\) invariant, so \(f(H_i)=H_i'\). Conversely every such \(f\) induces an isomorphism of the associative rings by using \(f\) on each core \(L\)-corner, its restriction on each \(H_i\)-corner, and the identity on all scalar modules and diagonal rings.

Let \(B=M_2(A)\). The group query is the class-two group \(Q(A)\) on \(B^3\) with multiplication
\[
(x,y,z)(x',y',z')=(x+x',y+y',z+z'+xy').
\]
Its derived subgroup and center are both the last \(B\), because the commutator bimap
\[
\beta((x,y),(x',y'))=xy'-x'y
\]
has zero radical and has image \(B\) by evaluating with the identity of \(B\). A group isomorphism therefore induces a bimap equivalence. The adjoint ring of \(\beta\) consists of pairs of additive endomorphisms \((S,T)\) satisfying \(\beta(Su,v)=\beta(u,Tv)\), with product \((S,T)(S',T')=(SS',T'T)\). Its two factors are \(B^{\mathrm{op}}\) and \(B\), realized by
\[
 S=\operatorname{diag}(R_a,L_b),\qquad
 T=\operatorname{diag}(R_b,L_a).
\]
Here \(L_b\) and \(R_a\) mean left and right multiplication. Substituting vectors on the two source axes, and substituting \(1\) on each axis in turn, determines the diagonal entries. Each off-diagonal entry would come from a common left or right annihilator of the ring commutators. Both annihilators are zero since \(E_{12}\) and \(E_{21}\) are commutators in \(M_2(A)\) and annihilating both matrix units on one side forces a matrix to be zero. This gives the displayed adjoint ring directly. [Heisenberg groups and adjoint rings, Lewis–Wilson](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5466)

An isomorphism of the groups transports the adjoint ring by simultaneous conjugation on \(B\oplus B\). Since \(Z(B)=R\) is local, its central product decomposition recovers the two factors. An isomorphism of either orientation would give a ring isomorphism or anti-isomorphism between \(M_2(A)\) and \(M_2(A')\). To restrict to \(A,A'\), consider \(E_{11}\), which has rank one in every \(M_2(\mathbb F_p)\) factor modulo the radical of \(M_2(A)\). Its image has that same property. Conjugate by a unit lifting the appropriate linear changes of basis in the residue factors. The two-idempotent form of the conjugating-unit argument in Section 2 now aligns the image exactly with \(E_{11}\). The corners at \(E_{11}\) identify with \(A,A'\). An anti-isomorphism is excluded by the directed graph. Thus every queried group isomorphism yields an actual relative Lie-ring isomorphism. In the other direction an isomorphism of \(A,A'\) gives one of \(B,B'\) and of \(Q(A),Q(A')\) entrywise.

All size charges depend on actual additive lengths. The core and fixed hub edges cost \(O(\log_p|L|)\) in additive length. Mark \(i\) costs \(\log_p|H_i|\) in its data corner and \(O(a_i)\) in scalar corners and diagonal rings. The path corners charge at most \(O(\sum_i a_i)\), and the pendant leaves and their arrows cost \(O(k+1)\). After removing trivial marks, both \(k\) and \(\sum_i a_i\) are bounded by \(\sum_i\log_p|H_i|\). Thus \(|Q(A)|=|A|^{12}\le (NP)^K\) for an absolute \(K\). The ring and group tables can be enumerated with the displayed formulas in time polynomial in \(NP\). The class-two query is always a \(p\)-group. When \(p\) is odd its exponent is \(p^e\), since the central term in the \(p^e\)-th power from the cocycle is \(\binom{p^e}{2}xy=0\) modulo \(p^e\) and the central copy of \(B\) has that exponent.

## 4. From group witnesses to relative automorphism generators

The recovery in Section 3 defines a homomorphism on automorphism groups, even though its computational description uses conjugating units. First consider the restriction from isomorphisms of \(M_2(A)\) to isomorphisms of the corner \(A\). Two choices of aligning conjugation differ by a unit centralizing \(E_{11}\). Their restrictions to the corner differ by an inner automorphism of \(A\). Alignments for two composable isomorphisms can be composed to give an alignment for their composite, so corner restriction is compatible with composition modulo such inner automorphisms.

Next align the named vertex idempotents of \(A,A'\). Two choices differ by a unit centralizing every named idempotent. Such a unit has a diagonal component \(d_i\) at vertex \(i\), because all off-diagonal components vanish if it commutes with every vertex. Its conjugation multiplies the map on corner \(i\to j\) by the scalar ratio \(d_i/d_j\), reduced to the relevant modulus. On the core, the scalar \(a=uv/w\) changes by \(d_{m_0}/d_{t_0}\), while \(b=u'v'/w'\) changes by \(d_{s_0}/d_{m_0}\). The map \(Z\) changes by \(d_{s_0}/d_{t_0}\). These factors cancel exactly in \((ab)^{-1}Z\). If one changes the initial ring isomorphism by any inner conjugation, one can undo that conjugation when aligning the vertex idempotents. Hence the normalized \(f\) is independent even of the ambiguity in the matrix-corner restriction. For idempotent-preserving maps the scalar parameters \(a,b\) multiply under composition, as does \(Z\) as a linear map. The same therefore holds for \(f\) in general.

We obtain a computable surjective homomorphism
\[
\operatorname{Aut}(Q(A(L;H_i)))\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Aut}(L;H_1,\ldots,H_k).
\]
Surjectivity follows from the ring extension of any relative Lie-ring automorphism described in Section 3. Its scalar units are all 1, and the entrywise extension to \(M_2(A)\) fixes \(E_{11}\). The two adjoint factors cannot be swapped by an automorphism because \(A\) has no anti-automorphism, and an anti-automorphism of \(M_2(A)\) would restrict to one of \(A\). The isomorphism recovery is also compatible with a change of the input to a matched target.

There is a direct polynomial table procedure for recovery. In the generated query coordinates, an isomorphism yields an explicit bijection \(P\) on \(B\oplus B\) by quotienting out the last coordinate. To read the transported \(B\)-factor isomorphism at \(b\in B\), take \(S_b=\operatorname{diag}(0,L_b)\) and evaluate \(P S_b P^{-1}\) on \((0,1)\). Its second coordinate is the transported \(b\). Invertible maps and units may be inverted directly from the tables. Alignment of the residue of \(E_{11}\) uses image and kernel bases of rank-one idempotents in the \(2\times 2\) factors, followed by the two-idempotent correction described above. In \(A\) the finite sums \(\sum_i f_i e_i\) align the full idempotent system. Read \(f\) on the \(L\)-corner using the displayed formula. The numbering of actual \(G\) elements is the same as that of \(L\), so \(f\) is already the required group map on those elements.

Apply the all-class-two black-box theorem to the query groups. Its search algorithm gives a relative witness by the previous procedure. Its automorphism generation algorithm, followed by this homomorphism, gives generators of the relative automorphism group as a permutation group on \(G\). Deterministic polynomial-time permutation group order computation gives the exact relative count when the relative isomorphism class matches. The count is zero on a negative decision because an isomorphism set, when nonempty, is a torsor for the relative automorphism group. The same yields the index of the subgroup stabilizer in the ambient automorphism group, which is the orbit size of the ordered subgroup tuple. [Schreier generators and permutation group methods](https://doi.org/10.1109/SFCS.1980.34)

For the simultaneous partial-isomorphism extension problem, start with a relative witness \(f_0\). Every other candidate is \(f_0 g\) for a relative source automorphism \(g\). Take the group homomorphism given by restricting \(g\) to the disjoint union of the \(H_i\), using separate copies even when the original subgroups overlap. Test whether the tuple \(f_0^{-1}\circ h_i\), for requested maps \(h_i:H_i\to H_i^\prime\), belongs to this permutation image. A straight-line membership witness can be lifted through the generating maps to an actual \(g\). Every successful request has exactly \(|\operatorname{Aut}(G;H_i)|\) divided by the order of the restriction image as its number of extensions, because the fibres are cosets of the restriction kernel. The same precomputation therefore describes the entire action on the marked subgroups, including its correlations between different marks.

Finally, each subgroup of a finite nilpotent group is the direct product of its Sylow intersections. These intersections are obtained within the given tables by computing element orders, and every isomorphism preserves them. Applying the construction to each factor and multiplying the resulting counts proves the stated odd-order class-two consequence. The relative embedding problem for arbitrary noncentral subgroups of nonabelian \(2\)-groups is outside this result.

## 5. A nonsplit example distinguished upstairs

Take \(L=C_{p^2}x\oplus C_p y\oplus C_p z\) with odd \(p\) and bracket \([x,y]=z\). Let \(G\) be its class-two Lazard group and use the actual subgroups
\[
H=\langle px,y\rangle,\qquad H'=\langle px+z,y\rangle .
\]
These additive spans are also subgroups under the group law because both internal brackets vanish. Their images in \(G/[G,G]\) coincide and both intersect \([G,G]=\langle z\rangle\) trivially. Neither subgroup is normal in \(G\), since \([x,y]\) lies outside both. No automorphism takes \(H\) to \(H'\), since the characteristic subgroup \(pL=\langle px\rangle\) lies in \(H\) and does not lie in \(H'\). Their common abelianized image is not a direct summand because its generator \(px\) belongs to \(p(L/[L,L])\) while the image itself is killed by \(p\). This distinguishes an actual subgroup mark from its quotient-and-derived data.

In this example the images of \(x,y\) under an automorphism have the forms \((a,b,c)\) and \((p d,e,f)\) in the displayed cyclic coordinates, with \(a\) a unit modulo \(p^2\) and \(e\ne0\) modulo \(p\). The image of \(z\) is forced to be \([f(x),f(y)]\). These choices give all automorphisms because their induced map modulo \(p\) is invertible and they preserve the bracket. Fixing \(H\) forces \(f=0\) in the coordinates of the image of \(y\). The ambient group of automorphisms has size \(p^5(p-1)^2\), the subgroup orbit has size \(p\), and the relative group has size \(p^4(p-1)^2\). Its restriction image on \(H\) has size \(p(p-1)^2\) with exactly \(p^3\) extensions per permitted restriction.

## 6. The three-generator class bound is sufficient

Let every subgroup generated by at most three elements in a finite \(p\)-group \(G\) have nilpotency class less than \(p\), and put \(b=\min(p-1,\log_p|G|)\). For any pair \(x,y\), use the ordinary Lazard correspondence inside \(\langle x,y\rangle\) to define their Lie sum and bracket. Inside a three-generated subgroup these operations agree with that subgroup's own Lazard operations, by functoriality under inclusion. Each Lie-ring axiom involves at most three variable elements, so the local operations give a Lie ring \(L\) on the underlying set of \(G\). Every subgroup of \(G\) is closed under the Lie operations on its elements. Conversely the degree-\(b\) BCH polynomial in the Lie operations recovers the product, since it does so inside each two-generated subgroup. Thus group and Lie-ring maps coincide, and the actual subgroup marks are preserved under the same maps. One may test the promise by generating the subgroup of each triple and computing its lower central series, all in polynomial time in the table order. The degree-\(b\) inverse Lazard word algorithm applies to every pair, with polynomial bounds as in Section 1. The Peirce and Heisenberg steps require no global nilpotency bound on \(L\). This extends the theorem to the local class hypothesis. Grochow and Qiao already point out the local Lazard principle for the exponent-\(p\) matrix-model reduction. The passage here includes Cayley tables of arbitrary exponent, marked actual subgroups, and the entire restriction image. [Grochow–Qiao, CCC 2021, Theorem P and §6.3](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2021.16)

The local hypothesis strictly extends the global range. For every prime \(p\ge5\) the following construction gives a finite exponent-\(p\) group of class exactly \(p\) in which every subgroup generated by at most \(p-2\) elements has class less than \(p\). Let \(V\) have basis \(x_0,\ldots,x_{p-2}\) over \(\mathbb F_p\). In the tensor algebra truncated above degree \(p\), let \(L_0\) be the graded Lie subalgebra generated by \(V\) under the commutator. On its degree-\(p\) component restrict the linear map
\[
\Phi(v_1\cdots v_p)=(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_{p-1})\otimes v_p.
\]
The kernel on that component is a central Lie ideal because every bracket of total degree greater than \(p\) vanishes. Let \(L\) be the quotient by this ideal. If a Lie subalgebra is generated by at most \(p-2\) elements, all its degree-one projections lie in a subspace of dimension at most \(p-2\). Any bracket of length \(p\) on its elements depends only on those degree-one projections. Its image under \(\Phi\) is zero since the exterior power of that subspace of degree \(p-1\) is zero. Thus each such subalgebra has class less than \(p\).

The left-nested commutator on the sequence \(x_0,x_1,x_0,x_2,\ldots,x_{p-2}\) survives in \(L\). The bracket on the first three entries is
\[
2x_0x_1x_0-x_1x_0x_0-x_0x_0x_1.
\]
In expanding the remaining brackets, every subsequent letter must be prepended for a word to survive \(\Phi\). If any such letter is appended, the last entry cannot be \(x_0\), so the first \(p-1\) entries contain both copies of \(x_0\). After prepending all the later letters only the first two terms of the displayed expansion can survive. Their exterior factors differ by a sign, hence their sum is \(\pm3(x_0\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{p-2})\otimes x_0\), which is nonzero.

Define a group law on \(L\) by BCH through degree \(p-1\). To test associativity on any triple, use its Lie subalgebra, which has class less than \(p\). There the ordinary BCH group law is associative and agrees with the global formula. Hence the law is associative, with identity zero and inverse \(-x\). It has exponent \(p\) since the powers of a single element are its additive multiples. Any at most \(p-2\) group generators lie inside the BCH group of their Lie subalgebra, so their group has class less than \(p\). The full group has class at most \(p\) from the filtration by least homogeneous degree. In that filtration, if \(u,v\) have degrees at least \(i,j\), then the group commutator agrees with the Lie commutator modulo degree \(i+j+1\). Indeed the correction terms have at least three entries and contain both \(u\) and \(v\). Iterating on the sequence above shows the length-\(p\) group commutator equals the surviving length-\(p\) Lie commutator, since there is no degree \(p+1\). The group has class exactly \(p\).

## Verification

The reduction is a written proof. Its replay exercises the normalization under changes of aligned idempotents, the marked corner rule on nonsplit mixed-order additive subgroups, and a finite example where marking the actual subgroup changes the answer even though abelianized and central subgroup labels agree. The replay also checks the exterior coefficient in Section 6 at \(p=5,7,11,13\). It uses small constructed examples and does not enumerate the large oracle tables. Publication priority for the relative result remains unverified.
